The maximum recorded total length for White margate (Haemulon album) reaches 79 centimeters [Li = 79 centimeters], placing this species among the larger-bodied members of the genus. Field surveys across the Caribbean indicate that individuals attain this ultimate size only after many years of growth, with the length-weight relationship suggesting a corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 5926 grams [Wwi = approximately 5926 grams]. Such a substantial adult mass reflects the species' occupation of high-complexity reef habitats where shelter and foraging opportunities support prolonged somatic expansion. Juvenile specimens, by contrast, are typically encountered in seagrass beds and nearshore nursery zones, where they remain until reaching a size sufficient to evade predation on the reef proper. The asymptotic length reported here is consistent with measurements taken from both artisanal and research fishery catches throughout the species' range, though local variation may occur depending on fishing pressure and habitat quality.

Sexual maturation in White margate is marked by the attainment of a total length of 30.5 centimeters [Lp = 30.5 centimeters], the point at which gonadal recrudescence becomes histologically detectable in both males and females. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty approximates 341 grams [Wwp = 341 grams], a value derived from the species' length-weight conversion and consistent with observations from histological surveys of mature gonads. Individuals below this size are invariably immature, suggesting that a minimum body size threshold governs the onset of reproductive capability. This pattern of size-dependent maturation is common among lutjanids and haemulids, where the energetic demands of gametogenesis require a certain reserve of somatic tissue. The pubertal length and mass thus represent critical demographic parameters for stock assessments, as they define the fraction of the population contributing to annual recruitment.

Reproductive output for White margate has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions. At a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum daily egg production rate translates to a substantial fecundity of approximately 6027 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 6027 eggs per day] for a large, gravid female. This value was derived from observed spawning frequencies and batch fecundity estimates obtained during captive spawning trials. The elevated reproductive rate is characteristic of iteroparous reef fishes that broadcast pelagic eggs into the water column, offsetting high early-life mortality through sheer numerical output. The thermal dependence of gamete production is well documented in haemulids, and the 25 °C [T = 25 °C] benchmark aligns with the mean summer sea surface temperatures across the species' core distribution in the greater Caribbean. At lower temperatures, both oocyte development rates and spawning intervals are likely to decrease, reducing effective annual fecundity.

The wet weight at birth for White margate is estimated at 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a value based on the egg diameter of 0.85 millimeters observed in the congener Lutjanus stellatus, from which the spherical volume and corresponding wet mass were calculated. This minuscule initial mass characterizes the pelagic larval phase, during which the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The newly hatched larva, measuring only a few millimeters in standard length, enters the planktonic environment where growth is rapid but mortality is extreme. The transition from this minute birth mass to the 341 gram [Wwp = 341 gram] mass at puberty represents an increase of over six orders of magnitude, underscoring the prodigious growth capacity of this species once it recruits to demersal habitats. The egg diameter used here falls within the typical range for haemulids, suggesting that White margate follows a generalized lutjanid-hatching strategy.

Longevity in White margate, based on mark-recapture studies and otolith ageing, extends to approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years] under natural conditions at a mean annual water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively long lifespan is characteristic of slow-growing, late-maturing reef fishes and has important implications for population resilience. With puberty occurring at 30.5 centimeters [Lp = 30.5 centimeters] and 341 grams [Wwp = 341 grams], individuals spend the majority of their lives as reproductively active adults, contributing to multiple spawning seasons over several decades. The maximum recorded adult body mass of 5926 grams [Wwi = 5926 grams] is typically achieved well before the end of the lifespan, after which somatic growth plateaus and energy is increasingly directed toward reproduction. Age-structured demographic models for this species indicate that the combination of delayed maturation and extended reproductive lifespan buffers the population against short-term recruitment failures, though it also makes the species vulnerable to overfishing of older, larger individuals.
